question.text: Is renal warm ischemia over 30 minutes during laparoscopic partial nephrectomy possible?
question.context: To evaluate renal damage and impairment of renal function 1 yr after laparoscopic partial nephrectomy (LPN) with warm ischemia>30 min. From July 2004 to June 2005, 18 patients underwent LPN with warm ischemia time>30 min. Kidney damage markers (daily proteinuria and tubular enzymes) and renal function (serum creatinine, cystatin C, and creatinine clearances) were assessed on postoperative days 1 and 5 and at 12 mo. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) was evaluated before surgery and at 3 mo. Renal scintigraphy was performed before the procedure, at 5 d and at 3 and 12 mo postoperatively. Statistical analysis was performed using the Student t test and logistic regression analysis. In terms of kidney damage and renal function markers, the statistical analysis demonstrated that at 1 yr there was complete return to the normal range and no statistical difference between the values at the various time points. The GFR was not significantly different before and 3 mo after surgery. In terms of scintigraphy of the operated kidney, the values were 48.35+/-3.82% (40-50%) before the procedure, 36.88+/-8.42 (16-50%) on postoperative day 5 (p=0.0001), 40.56+/-8.96 (20-50%) at 3 mo (p=0.003), and 42.8+/-7.2% (20-50%) 1 yr after surgery (p=0.001).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical case describes a study of 18 patients who underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy with warm ischemia time greater than 30 minutes. The study found that at 1 year post-surgery, kidney damage markers and renal function markers returned to normal, and there was no statistical difference between the values at the various time points. This suggests that renal warm ischemia over 30 minutes is not necessarily detrimental to renal function in the long term.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The study demonstrated that at 1 year, kidney damage markers and renal function markers returned to normal, and there was no statistical difference between the values at the various time points.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study doesn't explicitly address the risk of long-term renal damage, the lack of significant differences in markers at 1 year suggests that the risk is minimal. Other potential complications like infection or bleeding were not mentioned, which would have been relevant if the study had shown significant differences in these areas.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that patients who undergo LPN with warm ischemia >30 minutes can achieve complete renal recovery 1 year postoperatively. The data shows no statistical differences in kidney damage markers or renal function at 1 year compared to baseline, and GFR normalization by 3 months. Scintigraphy also shows recovery to normal values by 1 year.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Complete return to normal renal function markers and scintigraphy values at 1 year postoperatively
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No significant long-term renal impairment was observed, ruling out chronic kidney damage from prolonged warm ischemia

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The case presents data from 18 patients who underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy with warm ischemia >30 minutes, and despite initial postoperative decline in renal scintigraphy values, all renal function markers returned to normal at 1 year. This demonstrates that renal function can recover fully even after prolonged warm ischemia, making the procedure clinically feasible.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: At 1 year postoperatively, all renal function markers (including GFR, creatinine, cystatin C, and scintigraphy) returned to normal ranges with no significant difference from preoperative values, indicating complete functional recovery.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: The possibility of permanent renal damage was considered, but ruled out by the normalization of all renal function markers at 1 year, with no statistical difference from baseline, indicating no long-term impairment.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other options (A: yes, B: no) would require evidence of permanent dysfunction, which is absent here; "maybe" is the most cautious and accurate answer given the observed recovery.
